docs.title: Home
docs.text: Python library that generates rough 2D surfaces with a prescribed height distribution (rms, skewness, kurtosis) and spatial structure (correlation lengths, roughness exponent), plus tools to inspect them with static (matplotlib) or interactive (Plotly) plots.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.10 or newer
  • Required: numpy, scipy, matplotlib
  • Optional: plotly (interactive plots)
  • Docs and tests: mkdocs, mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings[python], pytest

docs.title: From PyPI
docs.text:
pip install nongaussian-surfaces                  # core + static plots
pip install "nongaussian-surfaces[interactive]"   # + Plotly

Install name: nongaussian-surfaces; import name: nongauss.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/BlackPianoCat/NonGaussianSurfaces
cd NonGaussianSurfaces
pip install -e ".[dev]"        # editable install: package, plotly, pytest, mkdocs

Extras defined in pyproject.toml:

Extra Adds interactive plotly docs mkdocs, mkdocs-material, mkdocstrings[python] dev everything above plus pytest, build, twine

docs.title: Virtual environment (recommended)
docs.text:
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install "nongaussian-surfaces[interactive]"

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
python -c "import nongauss; print(nongauss.__all__[:3])"
nongauss --help                          # command-line tool installed
python src/run_tests.py                  # from a source checkout: runs the test suite

In headless environments (servers, CI) use a non-interactive matplotlib backend: export MPLBACKEND=Agg.

docs.title: First run
docs.text:
from nongauss import generate_surface, print_report, plots

res = generate_surface(N=256, rms=3, skewness=1, kurtosis=4,
                       corlength_x=12, corlength_y=12, alpha=0.8, seed=7)
print_report(res)                                    # requested vs. achieved statistics
fig = plots.plot_heightmap_mask(res)                 # matplotlib figure
plots.save(fig, "surface.png")

or from the shell:

nongauss --skew 1 --kurt 4 --alpha 0.8 --out out/

Next: Guide for every function and option, API reference for signatures.

docs.text: Use moments to estimate parameters of a Johnson distribution.

docs.title: johnson_dist(coef, j_type)
docs.text:
Frozen scipy distribution for Johnson params (gamma, delta, xi, lam); None for 'ST'.

With Z ~ N(0,1): SU: xi + lamsinh((Z-gamma)/delta) SB: xi + lam/(1+exp(-(Z-gamma)/delta)) SL: xi + lamexp((Z-gamma)/delta) SN: (Z-gamma)/delta

docs.text: Draw samples from the fitted Johnson family (always dispatch on j_type).

docs.title: johnson_boundaries(skew)
docs.text: Kurtosis limits for |skew|: (impossible-below line, lognormal SL line). Above SL -> SU, between -> SB.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: nongauss --skew 1 --kurt 4 --alpha 0.7 --out out/ [--interactive]

docs.title: Concepts in 60 seconds
docs.text:
Generation has three steps:

  1. Spatial scaffold. A Gaussian surface with autocorrelation \(R=\text{rms}^2\exp[-(\sqrt{(t_x/\xi_x)^2+(t_y/\xi_y)^2})^{2\alpha}]\) is built by filtering white noise in Fourier space (the power spectrum, i.e. energy per spatial frequency, is the Fourier transform of \(R\)). It fixes where hills and valleys are. \(\xi_x,\xi_y\) are correlation lengths in pixels (x along columns, y along rows), \(\alpha\) is the roughness exponent.
  2. Height distribution. A Johnson distribution (a Gaussian variable pushed through a sinh, logistic, exponential or linear map; types SU, SB, SL, SN) is fitted to the requested (rms, skewness, kurtosis). The family follows from the numbers, you cannot choose it. Kurtosis can never be below \(1+\text{skewness}^2\); on that boundary the two-point type ST appears.
  3. Rank mapping. The pixel with the k-th lowest scaffold height receives the k-th lowest Johnson sample. The surface is then shifted to min = 0, so the mean is not a parameter.

docs.title: Generating surfaces
docs.text:
from nongauss import generate_surface, print_report, plots

res = generate_surface(N=256, rms=3, skewness=1, kurtosis=4,
                       corlength_x=12, corlength_y=12, alpha=0.8, seed=7)
Parameter Default Meaning N 500 grid size, surface is N x N pixels rms 3.0 target root-mean-square roughness skewness 1.0 target skewness kurtosis 3.0 target Pearson kurtosis (Gaussian = 3) corlength_x, corlength_y 10 correlation lengths in pixels alpha 0.9 roughness exponent; small is jagged, near 1 is smooth non_Gauss True False returns only the Gaussian surface invert False flip sign before the shift to min = 0 (also flips skewness) clip_percentiles None (low, high) clip of the noise; bounds heights, biases kurtosis down seed None seed for reproducibility

It returns a SurfaceResult:

Field Content z final surface, (N, N) array, min = 0 z_gauss the Gaussian scaffold j_type 'SN', 'SL', 'SB', 'SU', 'ST' or 'Gaussian' coef Johnson parameters (gamma, delta, xi, lam) msg fit warning, empty if none requested dict of the parameters you asked for

Related functions: gaussian_surface(N, rms, corlength_x, corlength_y, alpha, rng) returns only the scaffold; rank_map(z_spatial, values) applies the rank mapping to any two arrays. The legacy SAimage_fft_2(...) still returns the height array.

Check feasibility first

kurtosis < 1 + skewness**2 is impossible and falls back to ST (a two-valued surface). plots.plot_feasibility([(skew, kurt)]) shows which family a request lands in.

docs.title: Measuring surfaces
docs.text:
from nongauss import moments, hhcf_1d, abbott_curve, radial_psd, report_text

mean, std, skew, kurt = moments(res.z)
g = hhcf_1d(res.z, axis=1)          # G(r) = sqrt(<(z(x+r)-z(x))^2>) along x (axis=0: y)
pct, h = abbott_curve(res.z)        # bearing-area curve: % of area above height h
k, psd = radial_psd(res.z)          # isotropic power spectrum, k in cycles/pixel
print(report_text(res))             # requested vs. achieved table (also print_report(res))

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
Each plots.plot_* function takes a SurfaceResult and returns a figure. Pass interactive=True for a Plotly figure instead of a matplotlib one. Static figures have at most two panels and a white background.

Function Panels plot_surfaces(res) Gaussian scaffold, final surface (3D) plot_heightmap_mask(res, threshold=None) hillshaded heightmap, binarized mask plot_distribution(res) histogram with fitted Johnson PDF, Q-Q plot plot_profile_bearing(res) line profile, Abbott-Firestone curve plot_hhcf_report(res) height-height correlation along x and y, report table plot_spectrum(res) 2D power spectrum, radial spectrum plot_feasibility(points_or_res) Johnson (skewness, kurtosis) plane plot_compare(res_a, res_b, labels) two heightmaps on a shared color scale 
fig = plots.plot_distribution(res)                      # matplotlib Figure
fig = plots.plot_distribution(res, interactive=True)    # plotly Figure (needs plotly)
fig = plots.plot(res, "spectrum")                       # by name, see plots.KINDS
plots.save(fig, "out.png")                              # .png for matplotlib, .html for Plotly

Parameter sliders (interactive only; all surfaces share the seed so only one parameter changes):

from nongauss import interactive
interactive.explorer("skewness", (-1.5, -1, 0, 1, 1.5), N=96, kurtosis=4).show()

plot_compare is the quickest way to see what a parameter does:

neg = generate_surface(N=256, skewness=-1, kurtosis=4, seed=7)
pos = generate_surface(N=256, skewness=+1, kurtosis=4, seed=7)
plots.plot_compare(neg, pos, ["skewness = -1", "skewness = +1"])

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
nongauss [--N 256] [--rms 3] [--skew 1] [--kurt 3] [--clx 10] [--cly 10] [--alpha 0.9]
         [--seed 0] [--out DIR] [--interactive]
Option Meaning --N, --rms, --skew, --kurt, --alpha, --seed same as the Python parameters --clx, --cly correlation lengths corlength_x, corlength_y --out DIR write one file per plot into DIR (PNG, or HTML with --interactive); without it figures are shown on screen --interactive Plotly figures instead of matplotlib

python -m nongauss ... is equivalent. The report is printed to the terminal.

docs.title: Notes and pitfalls
docs.text:
• Axes. corlength_x acts along image columns (array axis 1), corlength_y along rows (axis 0). Before v0.2 the roles were swapped.
  • Mean. The surface is shifted to min = 0. rms, skewness and kurtosis are shift-invariant and remain comparable to the request.
  • Statistical accuracy. Achieved skewness and kurtosis converge as N grows; for heavy tails (kurtosis above ~10) use N >= 512.
  • Exact vs. approximate. Rank mapping gives the exact height distribution but the correlation function of the result differs slightly from the scaffold's.
  • Reproducibility. The same seed and parameters give the same surface.
  • Memory. Cost is O(N^2 log N); N = 2048 takes about a second and ~0.5 GB.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
python src/run_tests.py                       # all tests; extra arguments go to pytest, e.g. -k cli
python src/examples/make_readme_figures.py    # regenerate figures in mkdocs/docs/assets/
